overview: Three Department of State “List of Papers” sheets index correspondence and intelligence records filed under 894.727, “Telegraph Codes—Japan,” chiefly from 1940–1942. The entries concern intercepted, misdelivered, or supplied Japanese diplomatic messages; interdepartmental requests for coded communications and radio intercepts; Japanese contingency instructions during a possible crisis with the United States; and coded traffic involving missions in Southeast Asia and Latin America. A substantial group documents publishers’ and congressmen’s unsuccessful efforts to secure government approval to republish Herbert O. Yardley’s cryptographic memoir, “The American Black Chamber,” which the State, War, and Navy Departments considered contrary to national-defense interests. The sheets also supply cross-references to related decimal-file records not reproduced here.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, items 41–43: Pocket Books and Yardley’s memoir
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / archival index sheet
subfiles.about: An index sheet records June 1940 correspondence with Pocket Books concerning the proposed republication of Herbert O. Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: Pocket Books representative Robert de Graff requested the text of the Act of June 10, 1933 after being told that the codes printed in Yardley’s book had been changed. The Department indicated where the act could be found and subsequently advised that further publication would not serve the best interests of the United States. De Graff then stated that the company no longer wished to publish the book. The date in the page header appears to be the date or revision date of Form DS-46 rather than the dates of the indexed correspondence.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, page 6, items 44–53: intercepted codes and republication request
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / archival index sheet
subfiles.about: This index page lists records on Japanese coded communications and the Bobbs-Merrill Company’s effort to republish “The American Black Chamber.”
subfiles.summary: The intelligence-related entries cover telegrams intended for the Japanese Embassy but delivered to the American Embassy, Paterson’s International Code, Japanese messages intercepted and decoded at Bandung, code traffic involving La Paz, and Japanese diplomatic despatches from Bogotá. One intercepted exchange conveyed Tokyo’s instructions for a possible crisis in Japanese-American relations. The remaining entries trace inquiries by Bobbs-Merrill and Congressman Louis Ludlow and objections from the Navy and War Departments to republication of Yardley’s book. Several entries direct researchers to related decimal-file numbers.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, items 54–58: code studies, radio intercepts, and Chungking source
subfiles.doc_type: list of papers / archival index sheet
subfiles.about: An index sheet records 1942 interdepartmental code-intelligence exchanges, the final rejection of Bobbs-Merrill’s request, and information from a Korean officer supplying Japanese messages.
subfiles.summary: The Justice Department requested Japanese messages for code study, prompting referral of the request to the War and Navy Departments, and later supplied photostatic copies of Japanese radio intercepts dating from before October 17, 1942. Additional entries document consultation with the armed-service departments and the April decision that republication of “The American Black Chamber” would conflict with U.S. national-defense interests. A telegram from Chungking reported a Korean officer supplying Japanese code messages to the American Embassy; the Federal Communications Commission later advised that monitoring associated with this material could cease. The page also repeats a cross-reference to coded Japanese diplomatic despatches from Bogotá.

interest: The file is especially useful as a finding aid to the government’s dispersed records on Japanese communications intelligence, identifying intercepts and coded diplomatic traffic from Southeast Asia, China, and Latin America and preserving cross-references to other decimal files. It also brings intelligence collection together with publication control: the Yardley correspondence shows how State, War, and Navy officials treated an older cryptographic memoir as a continuing national-security problem. Particularly noteworthy are the references to contingency instructions issued during a threatened Japanese-American crisis and to a Korean officer in Chungking who supplied Japanese code messages to the American Embassy.
